Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to participate in this debate and I want to get as quickly and as directly as I can to the subject of the motion. However, I cannot resist the temptation to comment on a suggestion made by the hon. member for Halton-Went-worth (Mr. Kempling) in the course of his remarks, that this is not the time for Canada to seek to improve its competition policy. Why is it not the time for Canada to seek to improve its competition policy? He says it is because any number of businessmen in this country will indicate that this is the wrong time to do it, with unused capacity in the economy. Perhaps there are businesses that do not want to see the competition policy in this country improved, but those are the big businesses in our society. They benefit to an extreme degree by being able to concentrate their production.
There is more concentration in the Canadian industrial economy than in any other industrial country in the world. This is a very serious problem. It is not something, as has been suggested, about which we should be patting ourselves on the back. It should not be allowed to persist, because at this time there is a 70 per cent or 83 per cent unused capacity in our economy.
Recently at Queen's Park there was an example raised of coffee being produced and processed in Canada. That very product sold for nearly double in Canada the price it sold for in the United States. There are various reasons for this. There is sales tax, which is different in both countries. There is a difference which relates to the size of the store concerned. One of the reasons that the prices to the consumer are higher in Canada is the higher degree of concentration which exists in

the Canadian marketplace. Perhaps-that means someone in this country is making profits. I am in favour of profits. Profits is not a bad word; but higher prices do not necessarily mean higher profits. Companies can be less efficient, which is the trouble with having inadequate competition in the Canadian economy. There is not the same efficiency which would be produced if competition were taken more seriously and improved.
The competition bill has had first reading. It has been reviewed by committee. I am disappointed the hon. member opposite is not in favour of seeing that bill coming forward as quickly as possible, because it does and will improve the state of competition in our economy.

The jobs which have been created historically in that sector, since this country was formed, are the source of the standard of life of Canada today. More than any other sector, the resource sector has been the one which Canadians can thank for the major contribution it has made to our way of life, for giving us the industrial tools to open up new parts of this country, and for holding this country together as a viable economy.
I wish the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) had been present in the Chamber when his hon. colleague was writing off the resource business and indicating that it was not a business for Canada to be involved in, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for Nickel Belt has been on his feet continuously asking the government to support the resource industry in his constituency. He has suggested some proposals which were sincerely motivated, but some of which were unrealistic. These proposals were an attempt to make sure Canada remained in the resource industry. There is nothing wrong with the resource industry. If it costs $1 million to create one job, one must remember we simply do not want the creation of one job. We want the creation of jobs which enrich the standard of life for Canadians. The resource sector has produced that type of job for Canadians and will continue to do so, unless the philosophy being advocated by members opposite is adopted by the government.
Our objective is to get Canadians working at doing things which are valuable to them, saleable in foreign markets, and which will give us the necessary foreign exchange in order to purchase things being produced in other countries.
Turning to the concept of free trade, I should like to put forward some thought about that in the remaining time I have. Canadians, perhaps more than anyone else in the world, are attached to the idea of free trade. It seems to be more than simply an economic theory, as far as Canada is concerned. When free trade is mentioned as a concept, it has an ethical value. Canadians feel free trade is correct. There is a great deal in that. It is a philosophy which leads to a better international community which gives opportunities to developing countries to climb on to the engines of prosperity and do the various things other countries have done themselves. Some underdeveloped countries have developed to the point where they are able to give their citizens a high standard of life.
Developing countries have been too literal in their search for models and have tended to copy the example of eighteenth century and nineteenth century England. At that time the United Kingdom went through its industrial revolution, which was built on the textile business. Later it was developed into the shoe business. In various developing countries the literal message taken has been, "let us get into the textile business because it worked in England in the nineteenth century. Let us get into the shoe business-it worked in England in the late nineteenth century." The result of all that has been a glut in those two industries, which has caused serious problems for the
Trade
textile and shoe industries in all developed countries, in ours perhaps more than others.
I do not know very much about the textile and shoe business in other countries, but in Canada I know that these industries are in very serious trouble because of the glut that has been created by the developing countries copying that model. In a sense I do not think I have heard anyone in the House attack the government measures that have been designed to support these industries, but those measures adopted by the Canadian government for these industries-which, incidentally, I support as well-are not consistent in the long term with the kind of free trade goals for which most Canadians stand. So we have responded in the way that other developed countries have responded, with some kind of anti-free trade temporary measures.
There are other measures that operate against the goal of free trade which, as I indicated, is generally supported, as a concept by all Canadians. There are all kinds of non-tariff barriers which have been developed, and I think that in Canada perhaps the non-tariff barriers are far less significant as a block to imports than they are in any other country.
I heard last night from one of my constituents that his neighbour is an importer of cocoa mats. He told me that the importer was very unhappy with the government and that he would never vote Liberal again because of his experiences recently. I asked my friend for details, and it turns out that a shipment of cocoa mats from India arrived at the customs in Canada. This man had ordered the mats. He went down to start processing them. Incidentally, these cocoa mats are one third the price of the rubber doormats that are manufactured in Canada. They are not nearly as durable, but they are far less expensive.
He tells me that, in his opinion, the officials of the Canadian government were deliberately delaying releasing those cocoa mats so that he could bring them into Canada and sell them. "Is this the kind of thing for which the Canadian government wishes to claim responsibility, to make it more expensive for consumers to buy these cocoa mats, because it costs me $50 or $60 a day to be there every day, fighting to get the cocoa mat documentation approved to get the mats into the country?" he asked.
I did not know whether in fact the delay which he encountered was really caused by deliberate stalling as a kind of non-tariff barrier, but I was able to tell him some of the adventures which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) had related in the House about the difficulty Canadian farmers have met in getting products into the U.S. market, about how trucks full of strawberries and tomatoes going down to the U.S. market from Canada in the summer will be kept sitting for days and days while they rot, while documentation is examined and they are searched for marijuana and other products that are not on the list, in other words, by a whole variety of measures whose purpose, at least to the exporter from Canada, appeared to be to slow down trade.

The problem of the high number of unemployed in Europe will not be solved by increasing protectionism and closing the doors tighter, except at the price of reducing the standard of living of the people in western Europe, and I do not think that is a desirable option for them. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I speak tonight on this opposition motion. I consider this to be one of the most important debates we are going to have in this House in this session because the government has not really addressed itself to the question of the GATT negotiations at Geneva. It is also one of the most important issues which will affect Canada not only at the present time but also well into the 1990's and possibly beyond. I think that can be borne out by the number of questions which have been asked by members of the opposition over the past few months. I would like to deal tonight with what I consider to be the most important parts of the GATT negotiations at Geneva, and also to deal at some length with agriculture as it pertains to GATT and with what we in Canada would like to see in terms of our negotiations.
The long-term goal for the Canadian economy still should be one of free trade. That should be something to keep in the back of our minds. I believe it should also be in our minds when any policy is formulated, but the reality in Canada today is such that to pursue a free trade policy at this time would be in my opinion-and I think this is emerging as the consensus in the Canadian community-sheer madness. The following illustrates this point.
In terms of our total merchandise trade our country has had a surplus since the early 1960's, with the exception of 1975 when our exports were severely curtailed by the recession in the United States. On the face of this evidence one might conclude that we really do not have a trade problem at all. Unfortunately, this long string of surpluses in total merchandise trade has tended to obscure some of the rather alarming trends in the secondary manufacturing sector, and this is the area to which I would like to address myself tonight.
All during the 1960's there was an annual trade deficit in manufactured products of about $3 billion. This deficit has been growing larger since the beginning of this decade, and last year it was well over $10 billion. This worsening trade deficit in manufactured products cannot be attributed to just one or two areas. The sad fact is that Canada's trade deficit in manufactured products is getting worse in every single commodity group and with every important country with which we trade. Up until just a few years ago we were content to let our exports of natural resources offset the growing deficit in manufactured products, and this has certainly been well docu-
December 8, 1977

merited. However, in the past few years we have been jolted into a realization that our resources are not infinite.
The question which must be asked is: how much longer can we continue to rely on our exports of raw materials and semi-processed goods to offset our inadequate performance in our secondary sector? How much longer can we continue to ignore the number of lost job opportunities resulting from this inadequate performance? In very rough terms, last year's $10 billion trade deficit in manufactured goods translated into somewhere in the neighbourhood of 200,000 jobs for the Canadian economy.
The federal government's rationale appears to be that Canadian manufacturing companies are not competitive because the market is too small to provide economies of scale in manufacturing such as those available to companies in Europe, Japan and the United States. Therefore we should seek access to those markets, and the mechanism to achieve this is a reduction of tariffs and the removal of non-tariff barriers. This philosophy, in my opinion, is based on theoretical consideration, and it ignores the reality of world trade as it functions, and the realities of the economic environment in which we operate here in Canada. Canadian companies are not competing with French, British or Japanese companies but against the combined efforts of those companies and the governments of the countries in which they operate.
The negotiating strategy of those countries at Geneva are part of the industrial strategies of the countries, and those industrial strategies reflect the philosophy that a strong domestic base for industry is a necessary prerequisite to a competitive export position. However, in Canada we do not have that equivalent, articulated industrial strategy. In addition to this we do not have a competitive and economic environment from which to operate.
Trade issues for Canada are very complex but there are two outstanding matters that must be given serious consideration. First is the cost crisis, and second our proximity to the United States. I should like to deal with both very briefly.
Dealing first with cost, we find that material costs in Canada are in general higher than they are in countries with which we compete-those being the EEC, the United States and Japan. While the basic raw materials may not carry substantially higher costs, the semi-processed materials going into manufacturing carry the higher cost of wage rates, taxation, interest rates and social programs that are in advance of those in other countries with which we compete. That is one of the reasons why it is extremely difficult for Canada to attain a comparable standard of efficiency. Secondary manufacturing, in turn, has the higher cost of plant construction, equipment costs, labour rates, interest rates, and social programs.
The average labour rates in manufacturing in Canada are now about 65 cents per hour above those in the United States. Particular rates show an even greater spread depending on the various commodities and areas about which we are talking. We are therefore vulnerable to lower cost imports, and the $10
Trade
billion deficit in manufactured goods is a tangible manifestation of our problem.
In short, we are in no position to take advantage of the access we are trying to negotiate, and we are vulnerable to the further access we are prepared to grant.
Cost regulations on such matters as packaging and minimum wages, the cost of running the public service, the rapid and accumulated moves to enrich social programs, are all problems that we, as a country, must face up to and try to solve if we are to be competitive.
What is really being said is that we must get our house in order before seeking access to lower cost markets and before granting easier access to Canada for producers in those markets.
This brings us to the matter of Canada's proximity to the United States. We cannot talk about our economic position or the GATT negotiations without talking about Canada vis-a-vis the United States. In recent months several studies have been made on the cost of manufacturing in the United States relative to such costs in Canada. They all indicate that the cost to manufacturers in the United States is 20 per cent to 25 per cent lower than in Canada, and it is not the scale of manufacturing that determines the difference, as the government would have us believe. The difference is in the cost of plant construction, cost of equipment, cost of labour, cost of capital, and cost of many forms of taxation. The scale of manufacturing does have an effect but it is certainly not as drastic an effect as the above-mentioned factors.
If we were to seek a greater share of the United States market with the greater access that is being negotiated, I do not believe that we would be able to compete from Canada. The threat we face is that large, efficient, low-cost manufacturing exists today in the United States, and a significant cut in tariffs will make it just that much easier for it to sell in Canada.
In summing up our negotiating position, I do not believe that the government has conducted adequate studies of the impact on unemployment and on investment that will arise from the result of the current round of trade negotiations. This is one of the things that makes the Canadian public so uneasy when we talk about these negotiations and where they may lead us. What is of concern to most Canadians is that government policy appears, at this time, to pursue maximum across the board reductions in tariffs.
In the area of agriculture it should be noted that nothing has been done-no policy put forward, no idea about where we are going. The Canadian agricultural community is truly concerned that it could be traded for some industrial concessions. The agricultural community is also concerned that time will not be available for the government to put forward a meaningful proposal.
Time and time again members on this side of the House have asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) for a clear indication of what the government is preparing to do. I should like to examine a few agricultural commodities because

December 8, 1977
Trade
I think it is important that we review the situation in its proper context. I should like to start with that very important industry, the horticultural industry.
As expected, imports of horticultural products in 1977 will be over $1 billion, with further decreases in the degree of protection offered the industry due to the inflationary factor and our specific rate of duty. This is truly shocking for an agriculturally enriched country like Canada. Many Canadians do not realize the importance of Canada's fruit and vegetable processing industry which is part of the total horticultural industry, the one most concerned in our trade negotiations.
Although the total value of processed fruit and vegetable products in Canada in 1975 was $981,885,000 it was only 1.1 per cent of the total gross national product. To put this figure in perspective, it should be pointed out that the economy of such regions as the Okanagan and the Fraser Valley in British Columbia, southwestern and central Ontario, the Niagara region, and Prince Edward and Hastings counties in Ontario, the eastern townships of Quebec, the Saint John River Valley in New Brunswick, and the Annapolis Valley in Nova Scotia are, to a large degree, dependent on the horticultural industry.
In fact in British Columbia fruit production accounted for 36 per cent of the total receipts from all crops, and 12 per cent of all cash receipts in 1975.
The vegetable industry accounted for 53 per cent of the 1974 total farm value cash receipts from crops in the Maritime provinces and 45 per cent in Quebec.
It has been proposed on various occasions that Canada should concentrate on those agricultural crops with which it can compete on world markets, such as wheat, oilseeds, white beans, apples, and perhaps potatoes. It should be pointed out, however, that the agricultural industry in Canada is, by its very nature, regional, and only certain crops can be produced economically in specific areas and under certain conditions.
Before I leave the horticultural industry I should like to state that what it is really asking for is a degree of protection so that it could develop increased production and supply a greater portion of the domestic market. It is asking for fair tariffs, an equalization of tariffs. If this were granted and there was increased production, the industry would become more competitive on the export market.
The dairy industry is looking to the Geneva talks in the hope that fairer tariffs will be negotiated. The meat industry is seeking better access through negotiations to the United States markets and lower tariffs on processed and semi-processed meats. We would like to see greater access to the European Common Market for oil seeds, barley, and wheat. In terms of pork we would like greater access into Japan. These are all areas of concern to agriculture in the trade talks that are continuing. Up to this point, Mr. Speaker, nothing has been done.
What should our policy responses be in terms of our GATT negotiations? In evaluating the present government's policy

response, the conclusion must be a somewhat blind move to significantly lower tariffs. I would like to deal with two or three areas that the government has been looking at, and come up with what hopefully would be a conclusion.
If we move during these negotiations to freer trade, which means lower tariffs, it is my contention that many industries in the country would not survive. Among the ones that would survive would be most resource industries, any industry producing on a world scale, and some agricultural production- grains and oil seeds. While the above mentioned areas of the economy are important, they constitute only a small portion of our total economy.
The second option would be if we, as a country, move to a more protected market or increase our tariffs, and this would also be unacceptable. The eventuality of increasing tariffs would be that the tariffs would have to be increased from time to time to keep up the protection that many industries would become used to, and while this would benefit some industries, for the whole country it would be incorrect.
The third option would be a move to adjust our tariffs to be nearer to our competitors' level and, if needed, use the proper sections of GATT to stop dumping from other countries. In other words, what we should be looking for in Canada is not freer trade but fairer trade. This approach would place agriculture and industry on a similar tariff basis to that of other countries. While no one would deny that our long-term goal should be freer trade, it would be politically and economically stupid to lower tariffs significantly at this time. As an example, our horticulutre industry would be virtually wiped out.
The approach most appropriate should be an equalization of tariffs where necessary, coupled with a commercial policy to assist industries that need help, or to help industries relocate, if that need should arise in the coming year. A commercial policy that recognizes the burden of social programs, excess taxation, labour rates, interest rates, etc., is absolutely critical at this particular stage in our history.
In conclusion, I have proposed no profound economic theories, or no quick cures. What I have tried to state tonight is that the government must first inform the Canadian people as to what is taking place in terms of our international negotiations because they are so important, and then move in a realistic manner to deal with our tariffs as they apply to Canadian industry-agriculture and manufacturing. If this is done, Canada could move with certainty into the 1980's with a positive trading position on which we could build sound, constructive policies here in this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this evening we have a very general motion which really seeks to cover the whole waterfront in relation to a wide variety of domestic and international economic affairs.
It is difficult, in reading the motion, to distil from it its essentials. I shall not attempt to cover all of the issues raised by it. I do note references in the motion to world trade and to agriculture. That brings me immediately to a very crucial
December 8, 1977

matter, the development of a new world agreement on wheat marketing, including economic provisions affecting both grain reserves and prices. It will be useful this evening to spend some time on this subject. It is an important part of Canadian trade policy in so far as western Canada is concerned, and it is especially important for prairie grain producers who are facing a very serious cost-price squeeze situation, who are concerned about the development of proper and effective measures to strengthen their grain income positions.
Some very useful measures are already on the books in this connection, for example, the Western Grain Stabilization Plan, the two-price system for wheat, and the action taken this year to hold this year's initial payment at the same level as that existing for the last crop year. There are a number of others as well. The list of modifications and improvements in our grain production, handling, transportation and marketing operation in the past decade or so is extensive and remarkable when you take the time to consider it.
Taken together all of these changes give us a rather effective package of policies to assist prairie producers in coping with what otherwise could be an extremely difficult income situation. But one useful addition to that over-all package of policies which I would like to see, and which undoubtedly would provide Canadian grain producers with the most comprehensive protection against adverse market conditions internationally, would be a new, effective, and workable arrangement on world wheat marketing. Traditionally the development of such an agreement, including economic terms, has been a part of Canadian trade policy.
Sometimes our trading partners have agreed with us and sometimes some of them have not. Probably Australia has been one of our most consistent allies in this regard. In the United States the attitude has varied from time to time, but the present administration and the present United States secretary of agriculture, Mr. Bergland, have been positive, helpful and enthusiastic.
From a domestic point of view Canada's starting point in these discussions is important, and our first concern is the position of the Canadian grain producer. The farmer's opinions and aspirations are crucial. While the Government of Canada must formally be the international negotiator, the negotiation will be done directly on behalf of producers, and any world agreement we sign must be acceptable to and supported by Canadian grain producers.
Our basic idea is first and foremost the establishment of a range of prices which would be regarded as sound and reasonable by both exporters and importers around the world. To keep prices from falling below the lower end of that agreed range we would want to have a mechanism for accumulating excess stocks in a world reserve which would be stored off the market and not over-hanging the market in order to keep the downward pressure off the price.
Secondly, we would want all participants in such an agreement to help bear the costs of that storage because it is an advantage not only to exporters such as Canada, which would want to have an inventory on hand in order to be able to meet
Trade
the various exporting opportunities that present themselves, but it is also a very real and practical advantage to the importers of this world to benefit from a fundamental security of supply. Up to now North American farmers have essentially borne the world's storage costs. We believe that is unfair. We want to see the burden of those costs shared around the world among the grain trading nations.
Of course, at the upper end of the agreed price range which I described earlier, as we see the proposed agreement, the reserve stocks could begin to be released into the world's markets once again. That is the gist of the kind of agreement toward which we should be working. I suppose the fundamental question at this stage is-can we achieve it? I believe so. I am optimistic about our prospects in that connection. We made substantial progress in this past year.
The interest of the present minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board in a new and workable international wheat agreement goes back many years, to the late sixties and early seventies, just after he was first appointed. Unfortunately, some other major grain exporters at that time were not as enthusiastic. Early this year the minister responsible for the Wheat Board had occasion to discuss the situation once again with the new United States secretary of agriculture, Mr. Bergland. Mr. Bergland and the Canadian minister were largely in agreement about the desirability of a new world wheat accord and on the fundamentals upon which it could operate effectively. The ball finally was rolling in a positive direction after a good many years.
The next step was to have informal discussions with the Australians and the Argentinians to confirm a common view among the world's major grain exporters. Then the focus shifted to the sessions of the International Wheat Council in London. That council is composed of some 45 to 50 nations, the world's major importing and exporting grain nations. All the major international interests are represented there, with the one major exception of the People's Republic of China. It has proven, this year particularly, to be a very useful forum for the preparatory talks which have been going on toward what we hope will be the successful negotiation of a new world wheat accord.
For some weeks now officials of the International Wheat Council countries have been working to assemble the fundamental international basis upon which a formal agreement might proceed. It is Canada's hope that those talks will bear fruit within the next couple of months or so, in order that a final formal round of negotiations could be held in the late winter or early spring, probably in Geneva under the auspices of the United Nations. Canada is determined to do everything it can to help resolve any international differences which may exist so that these world discussions can prove, in the final analysis, to be successful.
In this effort it is useful to bear in mind that the sucessful negotiation of a new world wheat accord, which would bring a new measure of stability to world wheat prices, would also

December 8, 1977
Trade
make it easier for some countries to implement certain other commitments with respect to international trade which might be under negotiations in the MTN. The MTN and the international wheat talks are, of course, quite separate items, but if we are able to negotiate the new international wheat agreement successfully, that could have, in addition to its obvious direct impact, a positive bearing on the MTN discussions, making certain trade undertakings of certain countries somewhat easier to accept and to fulfil.
There is one further aspect of Canada's initiative toward a new world wheat agreement which deserves attention, Mr. Speaker. I refer specifically to the Canadian trade and diplomatic mission led by the minister responsible for the Wheat Board, which visited a number of Pacific rim countries in September and October of this year.

subsubtopic: TRADE-ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO ESTABLISH INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Work on the international wheat agreement was a priority agenda item for Canada to discuss in Australia, China and Japan in particular. In answer to the question just asked from across the way, I was indeed pleased and honoured to have an opportunity to participate in those talks.
A whirlwind tour like that one was, covering many thousands of miles in just a few days and including a heavy schedule of serious discussions, is an exhausting experience, to say the least, but at the end it is gratifying to be able to report positive progress in the work that has been undertaken. Our talks with senior representatives in the countries which were visited were encouraging and productive, particularly with respect to the development of a new international agreement on world wheat marketing. I believe we are closer now than ever before to the successful negotiation of a fair and workable grain arrangement, including provisions affecting price ranges and reserves.
In Australia we met with the deputy prime minister and minister for overseas trade, the right honourable Douglas Anthony, and also with the minister of primary industry, the right honourable Ian Sinclair, and senior Australian trade officials. In these talks we wanted to review with them the major elements of proposals for a new world wheat accord in preparation for the international talks involving both importers and exporters which are taking place this fall in London. We believe that it is important for Australia and Canada, two of the world's leading grain sellers, to have a consistent fundamental approach in this matter so as to ensure the best possible arrangement for our respective grain producers and the greatest beneficial impact resulting from the enthusiasm in the United States for a new world agreement. We were able in those discussions to confirm the understanding between Canada and Australia regarding the fundamentals of such an agreement.
In China and Japan the development of an agreement was analysed primarily from the importers' point of view. Together these two buyers account for almost one half of Canadian grain exports. It was obviously important to reassure our good customers about our intentions in this matter and to report on the work done to date.

In China we stressed our view that the Chinese, who are not currently members of the International Wheat Council, should join these wheat talks to represent directly at the bargaining table one of the world's largest consuming nations. Senior officials in the Chinese government have that suggestion under consideration and Canada is hopeful that they will give the idea careful attention.
In Japan we found support for the search for ways to bring stability into the world's grain markets. The Japanese have already involved themselves usefully in the discussions so far. Incidentally, it is probably also useful to note that virtually everywhere we went on the mission, buyers of grain commented upon the quality of Canadian grain as probably the best in the world, and expressed general satisfaction about Canadian grain delivery services. They were pleased to learn of our current plans to expand storage space on the west coast and to revitalize our prairie rail network, which will render our export operations that much more efficient. Canada is generally regarded as a trusted and reliable supplier of grain, and with the continuing solid performance of the Canadian Wheat Board I believe we will figure prominently in future grain trading operations in the Pacific rim region.
This mission to the Far East and the work I mentioned which is being done on world wheat marketing are of fundamental importance to Canada, particularly to the west, and represent, I believe, a positive, practical initiative to support and strengthen a key part of the Canadian economy.

subsubtopic: TRADE-ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO ESTABLISH INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we all know only too well, this country is faced today with an $11.5 billion trade deficit in fully manufactured products. Those are the products which produce jobs or, if we do not get sales, cause unemployment. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association has stated that if we can overcome this very large deficit we will be able to provide more than 800,000 new jobs for Canadians. That, Mr. Speaker, would just about wipe out the present very serious unemployment existing in the country today.
In order to overcome this huge deficit we must make our products more attractive to prospective buyers, both in Canada and abroad, in terms of price, quality and design. The reason we have this enormous deficit in manufactured products is that not only Canadians but many people living abroad have found that foreign-made products are lower in price and better in quality than those we have been turning out. They have been buying foreign goods in ever increasing quantities in preference to Canadian goods.
To make our products more competitive we must do three things. First, we must improve our productivity in order to lower costs and selling prices. Second, we must encourage more industrial research in an effort to develop new and more efficient methods of producing goods which are of better quality and more attractive design. Third, we should encourage our producers to make more trips abroad with the object of getting into personal contact with potential buyers and
December 8, 1977

finding out what is required to meet competition in the markets visited. The products which are turned out as a result of the information thus gained ought then to be displayed at foreign trade fairs and in the course of personal calls on overseas buyers.
To persuade Canadian businessmen to do these necessary things, the government must make available generous incentives, to be paid in direct proportion to the effort that is made and the results achieved. It is a waste of money simply to make large sums of money available to industry in the hope that the money will be used in the way the government wishes it to be used. The reason for this is because businessmen have three options open to them. They can pay out the extra money in additional dividends, or they can put the money into the company's reserve, or they can use the money to carry out the government's wishes. If the monetary rewards are paid in direct proportion to the results achieved, the government, which is the Canadian taxpayer, receives 100 per cent value for the money which is spent.
Speaking in this House on October 21 last, I outlined in detail the incentives I believe should be offered to industry to bring about the results which are necessary, and there is no need to take up the time of the House to outline them again at this time.
I would now like to deal with the trade negotiations under GATT. In the negotiations which are now being held under the world organization known as the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, the Canadian government has indicated it is willing to allow manufacturers in other countries to have freer access to the Canadian market in return for easier entry of our raw materials into those countries.
Such action as the government is planning at the present time, and which is being negotiated behind closed doors at Geneva, will make it much harder for Canadian companies to sell Canadian products in Canada because our much larger competitors have lower costs of production as a result of their much greater size. They can therefore undersell our producers and bring about higher unemployment in this country.
I want to remind the government that we must overcome this enormous adverse trade balance in manufactured goods amounting to more than $ 11 billion, which is the main cause of the present high figure of unemployment, 8.4 per cent, which prevails today. The kind of action in which the government is engaged in Geneva will make this figure considerably higher. It seems to me there is no check upon what the government is doing in Geneva. We are given no information by the government directly; in order to find out anything one has to talk to those who are actually taking part in the negotiations. In my view the government should advise the negotiators that the prime objective of this country is to overcome the huge trade deficit in manufacturing production which I have mentioned, and in this way to begin making available to Canadians the 800,000 new jobs which will be made available by so doing.

speechtext:
The fact is, Canada must play a part in these negotiations. It is no use fooling ourselves into believing that the world is ordering its trade arrangements in order to suit Canada. It is no use trying to delude ourselves we can avoid the consequences of being one of the largest trading nations in the world. If these negotiations were to fail, if we were to sink back into the kind of trade wars which took place in the thirties, the same disastrous consequences would recur. The consequences of a country like Japan finding itself barred from the markets it enjoys today by walls of protection, as far as the political stability of the Far East and the world is concerned, would be very dire indeed.
The fact is we are participating actively in these discussions. Any real analysis of the negotiations will show the protections being built into them, the complexity of them, and the objectives which are part of the tariffs. The objectives give us an opportunity to enjoy much greater trade. If we walked away from the table and indicated that we were not participating in this negotiation, because we were afraid it would damage our ability to export, the very reverse would happen: we would be cast behind our own walls attempting, with a narrow market of 23 million or 24 million people, to survive in a world well
1712

December 8, 1977
Trade
prepared to go aggressively forward and cut tariffs in this manner.
The Tokyo Round had four objectives when it was commenced. First, there was the reduction or the elimination of trade restrictive or trade distorting effects of non-tariff measures, and the bringing of such measures under more effective international scrutiny and discipline. Second, there was a significant improvement in the terms of access for agricultural exports. Third, there was an examination, as a complementary technique, of a comprehensive attack on all barriers to trade in certain carefully defined sectors, especially from the Canadian perspective where these impede the processing or upgrading of resources in the country of origin. Fourth, there was an examination of the adequacy of the multilateral safeguard system with a view to furthering trade liberalization and preserving its results.
The working out of the ways and means has been a difficult and complicated chore. At the outset there was the intent of the Americans to achieve deep cuts of some 60 per cent. This was countered by the expectations of the European community to have shallow cuts of some 25 per cent. It would appear the track being followed by the key nations now is that which is known as the Swiss formula, and perhaps it will be in the nature of 40 per cent.
As our economy has demonstrated, this is a difficult time for these cuts to be contemplated. Other nations face the same prospects and are voicing many of the same concerns. In addition to the level of the tariff cut, there has been a recognition that there must be a phasing in. In actual fact, the general phasing-in period is over some ten years. In effect it could be something in the order of 5 per cent or something a little more per year, if this were accepted. In any event it gives the nations of the world an opportunity to adjust to the cuts over some ten years.
Members of the opposition are failing to recognize that over the last year the effective devaluation of the Canadian dollar against the United States dollar, coupled with the very substantial devaluation of both dollars against the currencies of Europe and Japan, have provided us with a far greater advantage or cut in the tariffs of those countries than will be contemplated by these tariff negotiations, even after the ten year phasing-in period. The challenge is to utilize this opportunity we have with a devalued dollar.
We must not kid ourselves. The devalued dollar has a very high price for consumers in the importation of goods, and it is a painful dilemma for those who have regularly enjoyed the importation of goods. For those concerned, the opportunities provided by the devaluation, if exploited, can result in very substantial improvements in our trading position. Canadian industry has indeed demonstrated an ability in natural resource areas such as fishing and the products produced by western Canada. Great opportunities are already being exploited.
The hon. Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) indicated that last year Canada sold some 40 per cent more steel to the United States than the year previously. That

indicates we have competitive industries, and we are making great inroads in the world trade.
The published reports that are being made about our tariff negotiations indicate the exceptions which will be built into the program, the opportunities, the flexibility, and the fact that if Canada exploits its opportunities it will enjoy great trading advantages. The deficiencies we suffer because of our narrow population base can be removed. We can look at the major industrial countries of the world and recognize that there are great possibilities to be taken advantage of by us.
In these negotiations we are seeking the elimination of some tariffs of 5 per cent or less, particularly in our resource based industries. It is of interest that two thirds of the dutiable goods we sell to the United States are in this category. A more serious, thoughtful, and careful analysis of our trading and negotiating posture, and the actual realities of the Geneva negotiations, will show that we have great opportunities.
Apart from the tariff cuts there was a more important feature, that is, an attempt to develop a code dealing with non-tariff barriers. People I have spoken to in industry, in my own constituency and elsewhere, do not necessarily complain about tariffs, nor do they complain about imports making competition impossible. They believe the only reason some countries are able to sell in Canada is because of the artificial opportunities created by measures which are unfair and improper, and not because of the lower wage rates. On the other side of the coin, the difficulties faced by our exporters in markets such as Japan and other countries are the barriers which are occasioned by complex paper work and other things apparently designed to foreclose the opportunities for trade. The acceptance of a working code for non-tariff barriers by countries such as Japan will provide great benefits for this country and its export programs.
In tariff negotiations such as this, there must be a number of safeguards. It is essential to the negotiations that these safeguards are real, carefully designed, and enforced in order for Canada to deal effectively with the problem of its industries being victimized by imports dumped in this country.
I have attempted in a few minutes, somewhat informally, to view the areas of concern and to show that our friends opposite are not attempting to provide the House with the real facts, are not attempting to look at these GATT negotiations in a positive and optimistic fashion, and are failing to recognize that we are in a real world, not a dream world, and we have to trade in this world. We have spent our time telling the rest of the world what a great trading nation we are, that we are one of the great trading nations of the world. That implies we have to sit at the table and participate in trade negotiations. The fact is that the Tory mentality leads them to put their heads in the sand and let the troubles pass over, whereas the Liberal party, faced with the governing of this country, has to participate in these negotiations, to recognize its responsibilities, and to make certain that they continue successfully.

In fact it was very painful to recognize that here was a man having to say things which went against his grain and against his beliefs as he stated them previously.
We live in a nation filled with economic problems. We have a $9.2 billion deficit. That is more than the total budget when this government took power. We are in a situation where our dollar dropped to 89 cents this year, and here is the minister trying to tell the Canadian people that our economy is one of the strongest in the world. He is trying to tell the Canadian people that, by golly, it is a good thing that the dollar dropped that low. His reasoning is that it is good for our exports and that, when the value of our dollar drops, we can move our exports into the international marketplace. But what he failed to admit is that whenever there are exports, there are also imports. The low value of the dollar has affected our imports very much.
I was appalled to hear a man who comes from a rural, farming, ranching riding defending that kind of a position, knowing full well that the low value of the dollar is having catastrophic effects on farmers and ranchers in connection with the importation of farm machinery throughout western Canada and the Atlantic region. The truth of the matter is that when we asked him today what was going to happen to farm machinery, he said the Canadian people could buy from Versatile or from Co-op Implements, knowing all the while that those are two of the smaller manufacturers of farm machinery on the North American continent and that, even though Versatile is a Canadian company, the president of that company is on record as having said that he will not expand any more in Canada. According to the president, economic conditions in Canada are too poor, and any expansion of the Versatile company will take place in the state of North Dakota.
We witnessed a very sad performance by the minister who tried to convince us that we have a strong economy. If you took a look at the Financial Post of a month or two ago you would have found an insert the size of Time magazine which said that the reason why the Japanese are not investing in this country is that our labour wages are too high, we have too many strikes, we have lost our competitive position, and our productivity is down in comparison with that of other major trading nations. The same situation prevails in West Germany. But here we have a minister telling us in a speech written for him, that we have one of the finest and strongest economies in the western world. He knows full well that the people of this country know better than that, that this is simply not the case.

Just 20 years ago, 28 per cent of our gross national product was going into government expenditures. Under the Trudeau regime that grew to 42 per cent of the GNP going into government expenditure. The minister promised us a rose garden. Then he went on to smell, feel and pat the roses, all the while leaving the citizen out there nestling among the thorns. There is no justification for saying that Canada's economy is in a position of strength, especially when you recognize that when the government took power this country had the second highest per capita income in the world. Today we are in the tenth place, with Belgium one place above us in the ninth. No amount of rationalization, no amount of selective data, no amount of searching in a particular corner of industry, trade and commerce will justify saying that Canada has had a good performance in view of the tremendous slippage in the international market place.
I would be remiss if 1 did not point out how disappointed 1 am that, at a time when the economy is one of the major concerns of our country, the minister stayed in the House today only to give his own speech and to wander around occasionally. A few days ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) moaned about having to spend so much of his time sitting here because he has a bill before the House. At least he was conscientious enough to stay here while something of importance to his department was before this House. Today we are zeroing in on a major department on a critical matter, and I think it is a real slap and an affront to parliament to avoid being present.
We on this side cannot say that we love a 90 cent dollar. Canadians will have to pay dearly for imports. During the winter months more than one third of our food is imported. A devalued dollar means that every consumer who eats imported food will be paying an extra cost. It will not be possible to tell consumers that the devalued dollar is good, because it will have an obvious and definite sting.
We have an expensive government. This government has put us into a $9.2 billion debt. Who pays? People from Newfoundland to Vancouver pay. Of government revenues in this country in 1968, 34 per cent came from personal income tax. Of government revenues in 1976, 53 per cent came from personal income tax. The average personal income taxpayer has had to pay for this government's overspending and economic mismanagement.
This country is a land of hope but no promise. We are adrift without the rudder of a strategy for industry. This could not be better documented than by the fact that Canada, with all its educated human resources and mineral and other natural resources, pays $12 million per day in unemployment insurance. That is absolutely appalling. We spend $1.97 billion more on unemployment insurance than we spend on national defence. We spend about $4 billion per year on unemployment insurance in a country with the greatest potential in resources in the world. The government thinks that is acceptable. I am sure that was the connotation perceived by the average citizen.
This year's trade imbalance will be $11.5 billion, which in human terms means the loss of 850,000 Canadian jobs. The reason for this is a failure to adapt to the world market place. Regardless of what the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott) said a little while ago, the government has totally failed to recognize the shift in international trade patterns over the past ten years, the strengthening of the Japanese yen, the power of the Middle East oil countries, the development of the European Economic Community, and the strength of the American trade. While that was going on around the world, this country was preoccupied with internal matters. The Canadian government was talking about language and culture and forgetting that we had an international market place to keep pace with. I recognize that all countries need to be concerned about their internal problems, but never at the expense of their position in the international market place. This failure to be concerned about our economic position has resulted in Canada, as a nation, not being able to keep pace with the major shift in trade patterns which has taken place. That is one of the great downfalls of the government. It was so preoccupied with the internal self-consciousness of Canada that it failed to see that the world around us changed.
The Minister of State (Small Business) might try to show that he has the facts, but I submit to him that all he has to do is look at our status relative to our major trading partners to see that a country does not slip from the second highest per capita income in the world to tenth, behind Belgium, in a ten year period, without something obviously being wrong.
Canada has paid other countries to steal its markets. It does not make sense to close down cheese factories when Canadian Cheddar cheese is being rationed in England because there is so little available there. More important, the Export Development Corporation has been embarking upon programs which are and will continue to be a disadvantage to this country's
December 8, 1977

economy. The EDC gave $160 million to finance a pulp and paper mill in Poland. It supported that project in spite of the fact that our own pulp and paper industry is struggling to survive, and in spite of the fact that once the Polish people, with their cheaper labour force, start to produce pulp and paper for the international market, Canada will be at an even greater disadvantage. Today the minister attempted to defend that EDC action. He said that the Polish people can read, too. Of course they can, but Canadian money is being used to encourage industries in other countries which will hire workers in those countries and which will compete with our own industries at a time when we have a high rate of unemployment here. That is not acceptable.
Last summer the EDC announced that it would put $47 million into a mini-steel mill in Perth Amboy, New Jersey. That is not in Poland or in some Third World country. That is in the United States, and that brings to $100 million the amount Canadian taxpayers have lent to steel mills in St. Paul, Minnesota; Midlothian, Texas; and Sheerness, England. Meanwhile our own steel industry in Hamilton and Nova Scotia is encountering stiff competition and the prospect of further lay-offs in the Atlantic region, where the unemployment rate is already alarmingly high. The government argues that a Canadian firm got the contract to build the New Jersey plant, but that is merely a demonstration of the small-mindedness of this government. It says that if we build a plant in the United States, that will create Canadian jobs, but that is only for the short-term. In the long run we will have to compete with other countries which process steel. Those other countries will get the jobs, and they will compete with Canada, with the help of money lent to them by Canada in the first place. That also is not acceptable.
The Japanese have the strongest economy in the world. The Japanese strategy is to increase international sales efforts for existing products and to develop new products through government sponsored research. The Japanese spent $214 million over the last five years to help their computer industry compete with IBM's series 370. Canada has no similar program, but this year will spend $580 million on the CBC. I submit that when Japan tries to get its major competitive companies into the international market place they spend money on research. One of the things that Canada sadly lacks is that kind of competition research.
In 1971 foreign investment in this country amounted to $925 million. By 1976 it had decreased to $400 million, and at the present time we find that Canadians are investing more money outside this country than other countries are investing here. That underscores the fact that the average business person in this country has lost faith in the government and does not believe he can invest successfully any more. Canadian investors are transferring their money to other countries because the government does not have an industrial strategy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion which we are debating says in part that it condemns the government for its failure to develop an industrial strategy to govern industrial development in Canada.
I was amazed, Mr. Speaker, to listen to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) and the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott) talk so cheerfully about the economic situation in this country. 1 wonder which world they live in. Here we are with 900,000 unemployed. Those figures were given to us two days ago by Statistics Canada.
I have a report in front of me prepared by the Science Council of Canada, entitled "Uncertain Prospects", released just two months ago. I will quote from that document:
In 1971 the Science Council was especially concerned about the viability and survival of medium and high technology industries. In 1977 there are real fears about the prognosis for Canadian manufacturing as a whole.
Further on in the document it states:
It is apparent that the technological capability of Canadian industry has not improved. It has in fact deteriorated. Exports of technology intensive goods have fallen in relative terms, and many of the industries which produce them are unable to meet foreign competition in the domestic market. Job opportunities for scientists, engineers, MBA's, executives, and other specialists are scarce or non-existent. Government employment is frozen. This year's university graduates face the most dismal job prospects of the last 40 years. Human resources, which have been created at great cost, are being squandered.
That is part of an analysis by an agency appointed by this government, staffed in the main by business and university people who are not, by any stretch of the imagination, very radical. It will take several years at least to develop a successful industrial strategy, which we do not have at the present time. However, in the next few months this country will have to conclude tariff negotiations which will have a profound effect on our economy. The Tokyo Round of the GATT negotiations, which has been going on for about four years, is at the point where some firm commitments will have to be made shortly.
December 8, 1977

We have grave doubts that our negotiators have developed a successful strategy for this country. I do not even know how that would be possible since the government has given no sign that it indeed has an industrial strategy. It appears to us that the negotiators are bargaining away a good part of our manufacturing sector in return for advantages in the resource sector.
The most recent annual report of the Economic Council of Canada noted that there are no plans for industry to adjust once trade barriers are lowered, to which the federal government is committed. Indeed, the Economic Council said the element that appears to be lacking is a clear plan to foster the adaptation of Canadian industry to the trade concessions to which Canada would agree. At present it appears that the government is prepared to negotiate so that the winners in Canada are going to be in the resource base industries which export unprocessed and semi-processed goods. These industries are, by and large, more capital intensive industries, and the losers will be the manufacturing sector of the economy.
We have seen in recent weeks how poorly the resource industries have managed things for us. We have seen thousands of people laid off, with no prospects of jobs in the foreseeable future. In return for more concessions to the resource industry so that they can sell abroad, it seems to us pretty obvious that the government is prepared to sacrifice a substantial part of the manufacturing industry which, in most countries, is where the interesting, exciting and better paying jobs are provided, and especially in that sector of the economy where jobs have been disappearing at a steady and rapid rate.
It seems to us that the government is naive in its assumption that Canada stands to benefit from the next round of the lowering of trade barriers. If we were talking about real free trade there might be something to it, provided of course there were adequate transition measures to cushion these industries and those people who are injured. We are confident Canadians can be as productive and efficient as anybody else. To develop productive and efficient industries is something which we have not done recently, and which cannot be done quickly. It is our feeling that our negotiators, and we believe they are doing this in consultation with the government, are dealing with these questions in a theoretical way, believing as if by lowering tariffs then immediately Canadian industries will adjust to world competition and will be able to manage.
We have seen in recent years in old established industries in Canada, such as clothing and textiles, a very sharp increase in imports from other countries, countries in Asia and so on. Our industries have not been able to adjust. We have had some very desperate attempts on the part of the government in the last few months to reach agreement on so called voluntary quotas with these countries which are exporting goods to Canada. This has been done when our textile and clothing industries have been virtually driven to the wall.
In the New Democratic Party we have had some interesting experiences in the last few weeks. We have had groups, which in the past have not been very friendly, ask if they could meet with us and outline their problems, such as the Canadian Manaufacturers' Association and the Electrical and Electron-
Trade
ics Association of Canada. I have been here 15 years, and this is the first time they have asked to meet us.
We are not talking about an inefficient, old fashioned industry. We are talking about the electrical and electronics industry, companies like Northern Telecom. These people are very worried, Mr. Speaker. Not only are they worried about expanding, they are worried about maintaining the position they have and the employment that they now provide. They feel that major multinationals, particularly those located in Japan, are determined to break into the Canadian telecommunications market, and are attempting to do so on the basis of price.
They are not worried about fair competition. They feel that they are as efficient as any company anywhere in the world. However, they do feel that the pricing structure of Japanese companies is close to dumping. They point out that this is difficult to prove because of the complexity of the price structure in the Japanese market.
They also believe that while the Japanese are determined to break into our market, as they have broken into the market in the U.S. and the markets of other countries, they are not prepared to let foreign manufacturers break into the Japanese market. They have used, and are very effectively using today, non-tariff structures to keep Canadian, American, British and German products out of the Japanese market. They also told us that similar non-tariff methods are being used by te Germans, the British, and others.
They are predicting, Mr. Speaker, that this government's policies, this belief in freer trade without any thought given to what it does to Canadian industry and jobs, will mean a decreasing number of people working in the Canadian manufacturing industries which have traditionally provided a large number of jobs, indeed the best jobs in the country.
We are not opposed to the cutting of tariffs, but we believe that it must be done keeping in mind the real needs of the Canadian people in this modern society-
